concept.name: Reservoir Sampling

relationships.description: Connects Reservoir Sampling to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Reservoir sampling selects a uniformly random sample of k items from a data stream of unknown or unbounded length n in a single pass using O(k) memory.
spark.keyTakeaway: Maintain a fixed k-element array and accept the i-th incoming item (i > k) with probability k/i, replacing a random slot—giving every item an exact k/n selection probability without knowing n upfront.

concept.whyItMatters: Modern telemetry, log pipelines, and ML feature stores process millions of events per second where storing the full stream in memory—or running a two-pass count-then-sample job—is impossible. Reservoir sampling guarantees an unbiased, representative fixed-size sample in strict O(k) RAM and a single streaming pass.
whenToUse: Stream length n is unknown, unbounded, or too large to store in memory (e.g., live Kafka consumers, eBPF packet capture, API gateway logs).
You need a guaranteed uniform random sample of exact size k (e.g., 10,000 traces) for debugging, quantile estimation, or evaluation datasets.
Memory is tightly bounded (such as embedded agents or sidecar proxies) and must never grow with traffic spikes.
whenNotToUse: Total dataset size n is already known and indexed (e.g., a Parquet table or SQL table)—direct index sampling or `TABLESAMPLE` avoids scanning every row.
You need stratified or rare-class coverage (e.g., capturing 100% of HTTP 500 errors); uniform sampling will drown rare anomalies in common 200 OKs.
Sliding-window recency is required (e.g., 'sample from the last 5 minutes only')—standard reservoir sampling weights all historical items equally unless adapted with time-decay.
keyPoints: Vitter's Algorithm R initializes the reservoir with the first k items, then for each item i > k generates a random integer j in [1, i]; if j <= k, it overwrites reservoir[j].
By induction, after n items have passed, every single item from 1 to n has an exact probability k/n of remaining in the reservoir.
Algorithm R runs in O(n) time and O(k) space, calling the random number generator once per incoming element.
Vitter's Algorithm L optimizes CPU cost to O(k * (1 + log(n/k))) by sampling geometric skip distances between accepted items instead of rolling RNG on every item.
Weighted reservoir sampling (Efraimidis-Spirakis / Algorithm A-Res) assigns each item a key u^(1/w) (where u ~ Uniform(0,1)) and keeps the top k keys in a min-heap.

examples.title: API Gateway Payload Sampling at 50k RPS
examples.scenario: An observability sidecar needs to capture k = 5,000 representative request/response bodies per hour from 180M daily requests without knowing hourly volume ahead of time.
examples.outcome: Using Algorithm L in a 10 MB fixed buffer, each worker samples uniformly with <0.1% CPU overhead—eliminating OOM crashes during 10x traffic spikes.

examples.title: Weighted Distributed Trace Retention
examples.scenario: A Flink streaming job must retain k = 20,000 traces per window while prioritizing high-latency or high-cost transactions over fast health checks.
examples.outcome: Applying Efraimidis-Spirakis weighted reservoir sampling (`key = rand()^(1/latency_ms)`) across shards and merging top-k min-heaps yields an exact, mergeable weighted sample.

tradeOffs.pro: Algorithm R is ~10 lines of trivial code with zero floating-point math.
tradeOffs.con: Algorithm R invokes RNG n times; for n = 10^9 and k = 1,000, Algorithm L skips 99.99% of elements and is orders of magnitude faster.

tradeOffs.factor: Uniform reservoir vs. Time-decayed / Stratified reservoir
tradeOffs.pro: Uniform sampling gives an exact unbiased view of the entire stream history.
tradeOffs.con: Old items linger in the reservoir during long-running streams, under-representing recent distribution shifts unless periodically reset or exponentially decayed.

tradeOffs.factor: Single-node reservoir vs. Distributed mergeable reservoirs
tradeOffs.con: Merging independent shards of size k naively biases toward lower-traffic shards unless you track shard counts n_m or use priority-key min-heaps.

failureModes.name: Biased Distributed Merge
failureModes.description: Concatenating or uniformly re-sampling k items from two shards with vastly different traffic (1M vs. 10k events) over-represents the quiet shard by 100x.
failureModes.mitigation: Assign each item a uniform random key `u in (0, 1)` on arrival (or `u^(1/w)` if weighted) and merge shards via a global top-k min-heap.

failureModes.name: Stale History Domination
failureModes.description: In an infinite daemon, after 10 billion events, new events have only a k / 10^10 chance of entering, freezing the sample.
failureModes.mitigation: Tumble the reservoir per time window (e.g., hourly epochs) or use exponentially weighted keys `u^(1/e^(lambda * t))`.

failureModes.name: Off-by-One Indexing Bias
failureModes.description: Using 0-based vs. 1-based bounds inconsistently (`rand(0, i)` vs `rand(0, i-1)`) skews selection probabilities for early items.
failureModes.mitigation: Write unit tests over 100k trials verifying chi-squared uniformity across all positions `0..n-1`.

failureModes.name: Slow PRNG Bottleneck
failureModes.description: Calling a cryptographic RNG (`crypto/rand` or `/dev/urandom`) per event in Algorithm R saturates CPU at high throughput.
failureModes.mitigation: Use a fast thread-local PRNG (xoshiro256** or PCG64) and switch to Algorithm L when `n >> k`.

commonMistakes: Using `hash(id) % M < threshold` when you actually need an exact fixed count k—hash modulo produces variable-size outputs that blow memory budgets during spikes.
Forgetting that standard reservoir sampling destroys temporal order; if order matters, store `(arrival_seq, item)` and sort at readout.
Merging per-worker reservoirs without weighting by each worker's total seen count `n_worker`.
Using `random() % i` in C/Go/Java without care—modulo bias slightly skews large ranges; use unbiased integer range generators.
Applying uniform reservoir sampling to anomaly detection where 99.99% of events are normal.

sections.content:
## The idea

**Reservoir sampling** solves a deceptively tricky streaming constraint: how do you pick `k` items uniformly at random from a sequence of unknown length `n` in **one pass** and **`O(k)` memory**?

In **Vitter's Algorithm R**, you fill a `k`-element array (`reservoir[0..k-1]`) with the first `k` items. For every subsequent item at 1-based position `i > k`, you draw a uniform random integer `j in [1, i]`. If `j <= k`, you overwrite `reservoir[j - 1]` with the new item; otherwise you discard it.

By induction, if every prior item had probability `k / (i - 1)` of being in the reservoir, the `i`-th item enters with probability `k / i`, and each existing item survives with probability `(k / (i - 1)) * (1 - 1/i) = k / i`. Every item seen so far holds the exact same `k / i` probability.

## Concrete walkthrough

Suppose `k = 3` and events `A, B, C, D, E` arrive one by one:

1. **Fill phase (`i = 1, 2, 3`)**: `A, B, C` fill slots `[0, 1, 2]`. Reservoir = `[A, B, C]`. Each has probability `3/3 = 1.0`.
2. **Item `D` arrives (`i = 4`)**: Draw `j in {1, 2, 3, 4}`. Suppose `j = 2` (`<= 3`). Replace slot `1` (`B`) with `D`. Reservoir = `[A, D, C]`. Probability of `D` entering was `3/4`; probability `A` survived was `1 * (1 - 1/4) = 3/4`.
3. **Item `E` arrives (`i = 5`)**: Draw `j in {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}`. Suppose `j = 5` (`> 3`). Discard `E`. Reservoir stays `[A, D, C]`.
4. **Optimize with Algorithm L**: Instead of rolling `j` for items `6..1,000,000`, Algorithm L samples a geometric jump `skip = floor(log(rand()) / log(1 - W))` (updating `W *= rand()^(1/k)`), jumping directly to the next accepted item and cutting RNG calls from `1,000,000` to ~`21`.

sections.content:
## Weighted and distributed extensions

Real telemetry pipelines rarely run on one core or treat all events equally:

- **Weighted sampling (Efraimidis-Spirakis)**: For each item with weight `w_i > 0`, draw `u_i ~ Uniform(0, 1)` and compute key `k_i = u_i^(1 / w_i)` (or `log(u_i) / w_i` to avoid underflow). Keep the `k` items with the **largest** keys in a min-heap of size `k`.
- **Distributed / MapReduce merge**: Because priority keys `k_i` are independent of shard size, each worker maintains a local top-`k` min-heap and a coordinator simply merges those heaps into a global top-`k` min-heap—preserving exact global uniformity.

## Streaming sampling algorithms compared

| Algorithm | Time Complexity | Space | Weights Supported | Distributed Merge |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Algorithm R** | `O(n)` | `O(k)` | No | Requires shard counts `n_m` |
| **Algorithm L** | `O(k (1 + log(n/k)))` | `O(k)` | No | Requires shard counts `n_m` |
| **A-Res (Efraimidis-Spirakis)** | `O(n log k)` | `O(k)` | Yes (`w_i > 0`) | Trivial min-heap merge |
| **Bernoulli (`hash % M`)** | `O(n)` | Variable `O(p * n)` | Via threshold | Trivial union (no fixed `k`) |

## Failure modes and numerical pitfalls

Three subtle bugs commonly break production implementations:

- **Floating-point underflow in `u^(1/w)`**: When weights `w` are tiny (e.g., `0.001`), `u^(1000)` underflows to `0.0`. Fix: store `log(u) / w` instead, since `log` is strictly monotonic.
- **64-bit counter overflow or PRNG period**: In long-running streams, use `uint64` for `i` and a 64-bit PRNG (`PCG64`/`xoshiro256**`)—32-bit `rand()` cannot sample uniformly once `i > 2^31`.
- **Windowless stagnation**: Always pair reservoirs with tumbling/sliding window resets if the data distribution shifts over time.

## Where it appears in production

You will find reservoir sampling embedded inside **Apache Spark** (`takeSample`), **ClickHouse** (`quantile` / `groupSample`), **OpenTelemetry** memory-bounded samplers, and **PostgreSQL** (`ANALYZE` statistics collection using Vitter's Algorithm Z/R to sample fixed-size row blocks for query planner histograms).

## Practical checklist

- **Pick Algorithm L for `n >> k`**: Save 99%+ of PRNG calls when sampling small `k` from millions of events.
- **Use `log(u) / w` for weighted streams**: Prevent floating-point underflow and enable effortless distributed heap merging.
- **Use 64-bit PRNGs**: Avoid 32-bit `rand()` modulo bias once stream counts exceed millions.
- **Bound window lifetimes**: Reset or decay the reservoir per epoch if recent traffic matters more than last month's.
- **Verify uniformity with tests**: Run a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test over 50k synthetic runs to catch off-by-one bugs.

interviewProblems.title: Reservoir Sampling
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Reservoir Sampling. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

nodes.label: PRNG / Skip Gate
nodes.role: P = k/i or Algorithm L jump

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Reservoir sampling selects a uniformly random sample of k items from a data stream of unknown or unbounded length n in a single pass using O(k) memory.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Fixed Reservoir applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Downstream Consumer.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Downstream Consumer experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Assign each item a uniform random key `u in (0, 1)` on arrival (or `u^(1/w)` if weighted) and merge shards via a global top-k min-heap.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Maintain a fixed k-element array and accept the i-th incoming item (i > k) with probability k/i, replacing a random slot—giving every item an exact k/n selection probability without knowing n upfront.
Avoid trap: Using `hash(id) % M < threshold` when you actually need an exact fixed count k—hash modulo produces variable-size outputs that blow memory budgets during spikes.
Avoid trap: Forgetting that standard reservoir sampling destroys temporal order; if order matters, store `(arrival_seq, item)` and sort at readout.
When to reach for it: Stream length n is unknown, unbounded, or too large to store in memory (e.g., live Kafka consumers, eBPF packet capture, API gateway logs).
When to reach for it: You need a guaranteed uniform random sample of exact size k (e.g., 10,000 traces) for debugging, quantile estimation, or evaluation datasets.

putItTogether.title: Putting Reservoir Sampling Together
putItTogether.summary: Maintain a fixed k-element array and accept the i-th incoming item (i > k) with probability k/i, replacing a random slot—giving every item an exact k/n selection probability without knowing n upfront.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Reservoir Sampling before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Using Algorithm L in a 10 MB fixed buffer, each worker samples uniformly with <0.1% CPU overhead—eliminating OOM crashes during 10x traffic spikes.
